idiom_name: versioned visitor interfaces plus a bridge class (triple dispatch)
implementation_notes: The published Java answer (Tulach's APIDesign case study, drawn from the NetBeans expression-language API) keeps elements as interfaces and splits the visitor in two: nested versioned interfaces that list exactly the element kinds a version knows, and a final visitor class whose static factory per version bridges the element's dispatch methods to that interface. Adding an element kind means adding the element interface, a new versioned visitor interface extending the previous one and a new factory - no existing visitor implementation changes, and the compiler still forces an implementer to say which version it targets. The study explicitly rejects adding the new visit method as a `default` method on the old interface, because a default body cannot distinguish 'written against v1' from 'written against v2 and happy with the default'.
pitfalls: Versioned interfaces multiply: every added element kind produces another interface and another factory, and a visitor written against v2 cannot be passed where a v1 visitor is expected unless the bridge exposes both - keep element interfaces immutable and always add a new version.
A visitor that does not handle every kind must route to visitUnknown; nothing in the type system checks that the unknown path is not a silent no-op, so make it throw or record a diagnostic.

Bridging with an anonymous subclass per version is easy to copy incorrectly: the dispatch methods must forward to the versioned interface rather than to a concrete visitor, or the versioning collapses back into the classic visitor's recompilation problem.
Sealing the element interface (Java 17) contradicts the purpose here: a sealed hierarchy cannot accept new element interfaces from other modules, which is exactly what this pattern exists to allow.

variants.name: Visitor class hierarchy with instanceof re-dispatch and a virtual factory
variants.idiom_name: visitor class hierarchy with instanceof re-dispatch and a protected factory method
variants.implementation_notes: This is the literal Java translation of the Zenger-Odersky encoding: the extended element base overloads accept for the extended visitor interface, the extended visitor class overrides the inherited default case to re-dispatch new kinds (`if (t instanceof XTerm x) x.accept(this)` - Java 16 pattern matching removes the separate cast), and every visitor construction inside a traversal goes through an overridable factory (`newEval`) so extensions survive recursion. Java's class inheritance carries the operation's existing behaviour into the extension, which is what an interface cannot do: method bodies on interfaces arrived with Java 8, but an interface still has no state and no way to inherit a *class's* implementation. The cost is the overload trap - accept is overloaded rather than overridden, so the static type of the visitor argument decides which accept runs and the re-dispatch must be written explicitly.
pitfalls: accept is overloaded, not overridden: the static type of the visitor argument picks the accept method, so an extended visitor that does not re-dispatch in its overridden default case never reaches the new visit methods.
Every self-construction inside a visitor must go through the overridable factory (newEval); a hard-coded `new Eval(...)` makes all subclasses lose their extension during recursion.
The re-dispatch cast is unchecked unless guarded: `(XTerm) t` throws ClassCastException for an element from another extension branch, so use an instanceof pattern and fall back to super.visit.
